title: Backend performance review — benchmark ground truth
description: Expert-annotated truth for one benchmark repository at one commit. Three buckets, not one list: `expected` is what a competent review must find, `acceptable` is what it may find without penalty, and `forbidden` is what it must not report. The three-bucket shape is the point — scoring everything not in `expected` as a false positive would punish a review for finding something real that the annotator missed, and would make it impossible to express a healthy repository, whose correct answer is an empty `expected` and a populated `forbidden`.

commit.description: Ground truth is only true at a commit. Annotations without one silently rot.

workload.description: The workload the annotation assumes. A finding's severity is only defensible relative to one.

method.description: How the truth was established. `blind-pass-derived` means it was retro-annotated from a recorded independent review rather than established first — weaker, and it must say so.

expected.description: Findings a competent review must produce. Each miss is a false negative.

acceptable.description: Real issues that a review may report without penalty and is not required to find. Scored neither way. This is where a genuine finding the annotator did not consider important enough to require belongs.

forbidden.description: Things a review must NOT report — the false-positive traps. A pattern that looks like a problem and provably is not: a loop over a fixed configuration list, a query on a table bounded to a handful of rows, an unused code path. A healthy repository is expressed as an empty `expected` and a populated `forbidden`.

also_locations.description: Other files a reasonable reviewer might cite as this finding's location instead of `location` — added after two independent real reviews of the identical bug (a per-item query reached through a call chain) legitimately cited opposite ends of the chain: one the query-issuing method's definition site, the other the call site that would actually need to change. Neither citation is more correct than the other, and picking a single canonical file as `location` makes the choice you did not pick score as a miss. A match against any entry here counts the same as a match against `location`.

also_acceptable_categories.description: Categories a reasonable reviewer might file this under instead. A pool-exhaustion finding filed as `concurrency` rather than `data-access` is not a miss.

mechanism.description: What is actually wrong, in one line. Used by a human comparing results, not by the matcher.

severity.description: Expert severity, for calibration scoring. Agreement is measured as exact, within one level, or a large disagreement.

max_confidence.description: The best grade the available evidence can support. A review claiming `Confirmed` where no runtime artifact exists is wrong however right the finding is.

expected_recommendation.description: Keywords that a correct fix would mention. Crude on purpose — it catches recommending a cache where the work should have been removed, which is the failure worth catching.

forbidden_recommendation.description: Keywords indicating a cargo-cult fix for this specific finding.

why_not.description: Why reporting this would be wrong. Must be a fact about the code, not an opinion — the counter-evidence a review should have found.
